passage:
In the school office, Darshan Mama slid the fee receipt across the counter. "Third term, and again from my pocket," he told the clerk, loud enough for the queue to hear. "Family must help family."
Urmila stood beside him, her face warm. She was grateful, she really was. She also wanted the floor to open.
"Thank you, Mama," she said. "Truly. I'll make it count, and one day I'll pay it back."
He smiled and patted her head as if that settled it.
At home she asked Amma, "Could you tell Mama we're thankful, but he needn't say it in front of people?"
Amma sighed. "I'll talk to him gently. He means well, but we should say something."
Urmila went back to her homework, still feeling two things at once.

qa.q: What did Darshan Mama tell the clerk?
qa.a: He said it was the third term and again from his pocket, and that family must help family.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Urmila have in the office?
qa.a: She felt grateful, but she was also humiliated and wanted the floor to open.

qa.q: What could Urmila and her parents do about the reminders?
qa.a: Urmila can keep thanking Mama sincerely and plan to repay him one day, while Amma gently asks him not to mention the fees in public.

qa.q: How might Darshan Mama see his remark to the clerk?
qa.a: He may see it as ordinary family duty said with a good heart, without noticing that it embarrasses Urmila.

grounding: A relative pays the fees and reminds everyone of it; the teen feels gratitude and humiliation, thanks him and asks her parent to set a gentle boundary.

passage:
Dear Maa,
I didn't want to say this in front of everyone at Diwali, so I'm writing instead.
I'm really grateful to Vasudha Mausi for paying my school fees these two years. I know we couldn't have managed. I'm going to thank her properly, and one day I want to do the same for someone.
But Maa, every time we visit, she mentions it. 'Study hard, I'm paying, remember.' At Diwali she said it in front of all the cousins, and I wanted to disappear. I felt thankful and small at the same time, and I hate feeling both.
I'm not asking you to fight with her. Could you, gently, tell her how it feels for us? Maybe that we know, we'll never forget, and she doesn't need to remind us?
I'll write her a thank-you card this week. I just need your help with the rest.
Love,
Abhinav

qa.q: What does Vasudha Mausi say on every visit?
What does Abhinav feel when Mausi mentions the fees?
qa.a: Abhinav feels grateful and humiliated at once, wanting to disappear when it's said in front of the cousins.

qa.q: What makes Abhinav's plan a balanced one?
qa.a: Abhinav will thank Mausi sincerely with a card and asks Maa to set a gentle boundary, instead of fighting.

qa.q: How might Vasudha Mausi see her reminders?
qa.a: She may think she's motivating Abhinav, not realising the reminders feel humiliating.

grounding: A letter from a teen grateful yet humiliated by a relative who pays fees and keeps mentioning it, planning to thank her and asking a parent to set a boundary.

passage: Chinmay, you asked why I went so quiet at Jethu's place last Sunday. I'll tell you, since you're the only one who won't make it a joke. I'm Arnab, the lucky nephew, remember? Jethu pays my hostel fees. At every family lunch he says it: 'Arnab, this fish is from my pocket too, eh?' Everyone laughs. I laugh. And inside I feel two things at once: thankful, because without him I'd be out of school, and humiliated, because Baba stares at his plate every time. So this week I did two things. I wrote Jethu a proper thank-you letter and told him I'll pay it forward to some kid someday. And I asked Baba, gently, if he could ask Jethu to stop saying it at lunch. Baba went red, then said he'd been wanting to for months. He talked to Jethu yesterday. Fingers crossed for next Sunday.

qa.q: What does Jethu say at every family lunch?
qa.a: 'Arnab, this fish is from my pocket too, eh?'

qa.q: What two feelings does Arnab describe?
qa.a: He feels thankful that Jethu keeps him in school and humiliated when it's joked about at lunch.

qa.q: Which two steps did Arnab take, and why are they wise?
qa.a: He wrote Jethu a sincere thank-you and asked Baba to set a gentle boundary, keeping both gratitude and dignity.

qa.q: How does Baba seem to feel at those lunches?
qa.a: He seems ashamed, staring at his plate, and relieved when Arnab gives him a reason to speak to Jethu.

grounding: A spoken account of a teen grateful yet humiliated by an uncle paying fees and reminding them, thanking him and asking a parent to set a boundary.
